blocks.label: PENDING: read before the exam
blocks.text:
Still to be taught. Do in this order.
1. HOLT (pages 22-36), exam critical, asked in 2 exams. Formulas: Lt = α·Yt + (1-α)(L(t-1)+T(t-1)); Tt = β(Lt-L(t-1)) + (1-β)T(t-1); F(t+1) = Lt + Tt; F(t+k) = Lt + k·Tt. Idea: SES lags on a trend, Holt tracks the slope T. Always compute L first, then T. Problems: (a) Mar 2026 makeup Q6 (weeks 1-7 demand 20..32, α=0.4, β=0.3, L1=20, T1=2: every L and T comes out clean, F8 = 34, 5M, part c is the why-Holt-over-SES reason); (b) Sept 2025 regular (L0=15, T0=3, α=0.5, β=0.3, subscriptions 15,18,22,25,29,33 for Jan-Jun, forecast July). Also the special cases α or β = 0 or 1 (pages 28-33) and remember Holt is not Holt-Winters (no seasonal part).
2. Moving averages (pages 16-21): asked in 2023 and the Mar 2026 makeup (3-year MA gave 51 for 2025).
3. Model slides (pages 67-82): AR(1) 37, 27.9, 21.53; ARMA(1,1) 8.8, 7.4; ARIMA(1,1,1) 122.3, 123.22; SARIMA 165 then 137; SARIMAX 42 vs 34; VAR(1) 1.6%, 2.4%; VARMAX 1.735%; comparison table p.82. No past paper asks these.
4. Holt-Winters and decomposition (pages 37-66): skim, no question seen.

blocks.label: Check against the slides
blocks.text: Some videos write F(t) = F(t−1) + α(A(t−1) − F(t−1)). It is the same formula as the slides' F(t+1) = αYt + (1 − α)Ft. For Holt, the starting level and trend differ between videos; in the exam they are given.

lesson.title: What this chapter is trying to do
lesson.lead: Predict the next value of a series by blending what just happened with what you predicted last time.

blocks.text: Simple exponential smoothing (SES) is a weighted average of all the past values, with exponentially decreasing importance for older values. In practice you never average everything: each new forecast is a blend of the latest actual value and the previous forecast, and α sets the blend.

F2 = Y1
F(t+1) = α × Yt + (1 − α) × Ft
blocks.caption: pages 3-4

head: α
What it does
Page
rows: The forecast is just the last actual value: a naive forecast
The forecast is just the previous forecast
Gives less weight to the current value: a smoother series
Gives more weight to the current value: a more variable series that reacts faster

blocks.text: The flow for any SES question

items: Read the start rule. 'Initial forecast equals the first actual' means F(first period) = Y(first period).
Write α and 1 − α.
Build a table row by row: the new forecast uses the previous row's actual and the previous row's forecast.
Go one row past the data if they ask for the next period.
If they ask which α is better: error = actual − forecast for every period, square it, add, divide by the number of periods (MSE), and pick the smaller.
Write one line of justification.

blocks.label: Check yourself
blocks.text: F(first) and F(second) are equal when the initial forecast equals the first actual, because F2 = α·Y1 + (1 − α)·F1 = Y1.

lesson.title: Measuring forecast error (pages 8-9)
lesson.lead: To choose between two forecasts, add up how wrong each one was.

blocks.text: error in period t = actual − forecast = Yt − Ft

head: Measure
What it is
rows: Mean Square Error: average of the squared errors
Mean Absolute Deviation: average of the absolute errors
Mean Absolute Percent Error: average of |error| / actual
Largest Absolute Deviation: the biggest single |error|

blocks.text: MSE = {{ Σ (Yt − Ft)² // number of periods }}

blocks.label: A caution about the slides' table (pages 11-15)
blocks.text: The utilization table on pages 11-15 gives each row the smoothed value that already includes that row's actual Y, and then compares the two. That is not a true forecast error. A proper one-step forecast error gives larger MSEs (3.59, 2.24 and 1.47 when I recomputed them). The ranking is the same: α = 0.7 is the best. The Feb 2026 answer key uses the page 4 form, so use that in the exam. Pages 5-7 are images that I could not read.

blocks.label: Convention to state
blocks.text: When the initial forecast equals the first actual, the first year's error is 0. The slides' page 12 table averages over all rows including that 0 row. If you divide by n − 1 instead the MSE is larger, but the ranking of two α values does not change. Say which you used.

worked.title: SES · Feb 2026 end-sem Q2: monthly demand (5 marks)

problem.text: A logistics company uses Simple Exponential Smoothing to forecast monthly demand for a machine-learning inference service deployed on cloud servers. The demand (in thousands of requests) for the past six months is shown below. [5 marks]

The initial forecast for January is assumed to be equal to the actual demand in January. (i) Forecast the demand for July using α = 0.4. (ii) Forecast the demand for July using α = 0.7. (iii) Briefly comment on which α value is more suitable if sudden spikes in demand are expected in real-time AI applications. All calculations must be shown clearly. Use Simple Exponential Smoothing only.

steps.label: Keywords
steps.text: Simple exponential smoothing, smoothing constant α, initial forecast = January actual, forecast for July (one month after the data ends), sudden spikes.

steps.label: Formula (page 4)
steps.text: F(t+1) = α·Yt + (1 − α)·Ft. New forecast = α × (latest actual) + (1 − α) × (last forecast).

steps.label: Start
steps.text: F(Jan) = 82, because the question says so. Then F(Feb) = α·82 + (1 − α)·82 = 82.

steps.label: (iii) Which α for spikes
steps.text: **α = 0.7.** It puts 70% of the weight on the latest actual value, so it reacts quickly to a spike. α = 0.4 keeps 60% on the old forecast, so it reacts slowly. Check: demand is rising to 102, and 99.88 is closer to it than 96.37. As extra support, the average squared error for Feb to Jun is 32.9 for α = 0.7 and 56.5 for α = 0.4.

steps.label: Where marks are lost
steps.text: Using the actuals and forecasts the wrong way round; forgetting F(Jan) = F(Feb) = 82; stopping at June when the question asks for July.

worked.answer: F(July) ≈ 96.37 for α = 0.4 and ≈ 99.88 for α = 0.7. α = 0.7 is more suitable for spikes because it reacts faster to recent changes.

worked.title: SES · Sept 2025 end-sem Q2: rice exports, MSE comparison (8 marks)

problem.text: The following data relates to the export of rice (in thousands of quintals) to USA from 2015 to 2021. [8 marks]

Using the Simple Exponential Smoothing technique: (i) Forecast the export for the year 2022 using α = 0.3, assuming the initial forecast for 2015 is equal to the actual export value in that year. (ii) Forecast the export for 2022 using α = 0.6, with the same initial condition. (iii) Determine which of the two smoothing constants (α = 0.3 or α = 0.6) provides a better forecast based on Mean Squared Error (MSE) and justify your answer.

steps.label: Keywords
steps.text: Simple exponential smoothing, initial forecast for 2015 = actual, forecast for 2022 (one year past the data), MSE.

steps.label: Formulas
steps.text: F(t+1) = α·Yt + (1 − α)·Ft. Error = Yt − Ft. MSE = Σ(error²) / number of years (pages 4, 8-9, 12).

steps.label: (iii) Which is better
steps.text: **α = 0.6, because its MSE is smaller (202.94 < 210.33).** The series jumps and drops (174 to 140 in 2020), and a larger α follows recent changes more closely.

steps.label: Convention
steps.text: The first year's error is 0 (forecast set equal to the actual), and I divided by all 7 years as the slides' page 12 table does. Dividing by 6 gives 245.38 and 236.77; the ranking is the same. State which you used. There is no answer key for this paper, so these numbers are my calculations, checked two ways.

steps.label: Where marks are lost
steps.text: Writing F2016 as 159 instead of 146; swapping α and 1 − α; stopping at 2021 when the question asks for 2022.

worked.title: SES · 2023 end-sem Q3a: monthly sales, choose the best α (5 marks)

problem.text: Consider the following time series data. [5 marks]

Assuming the forecast for the month of January as 50, fit exponential smoothing models to the above data with a smoothing parameter α = 0.10 and α = 0.70. Choose the best model between these two and forecast the sales for the month of June.

steps.label: Keywords
steps.text: Exponential smoothing, forecast for January = 50 (the start), two α values, 'choose the best model' (so you need an error measure), forecast June (one month past the data).

steps.label: Formulas
steps.text: F(t+1) = α·Yt + (1 − α)·Ft. Error = Yt − Ft. MSE = Σ error² / n. The question names no error measure, so use MSE (pages 8-9) and say so.

steps.label: Choose the best model
steps.text: **α = 0.70, because its MSE is smaller (4.07 < 14.74).** The same answer comes from the mean absolute deviation (1.78 for α = 0.7 against 3.24 for α = 0.1). Reason: sales rise steadily, and a larger α follows the latest values more closely.

steps.label: Forecast for June
steps.text: From the best model (α = 0.70): **about 56.24 lakhs.**

steps.label: Why every error is positive
steps.text: Sales keep rising, so SES (which only tracks the level) always forecasts too low. That lag is exactly what Holt's method fixes with a trend term.

steps.label: Convention
steps.text: The first month's error is 0 (forecast set equal to the actual) and I divided by all 5 months. Dividing by 4 gives 18.43 and 5.09; the ranking is the same. State which you used. There is no answer key for this paper, so the numbers are my calculations, checked by recomputing.

worked.answer: F(June) ≈ 51.62 for α = 0.10 and ≈ 56.24 for α = 0.70. α = 0.70 is the better model (MSE 4.07 vs 14.74), so the June forecast is about 56.24 lakhs.

worked.title: SES · Practice 5.2: update the forecast when the new actual arrives

problem.text: The number of weekly visitors over the last 5 weeks was: 1500, 1750, 1600, 1800, 1700. (a) Forecast visitors for week 6 using exponential smoothing with α = 0.3. (b) If the actual visitors in week 6 was 1850, what is the forecast for week 7?

steps.label: Keywords
steps.text: Exponential smoothing, α = 0.3, forecast week 6, then a new actual arrives and you forecast week 7. The slides' start rule: F2 = Y1 (page 4).

steps.label: What this teaches
steps.text: Each time a real actual arrives, you use it in the next forecast and carry the old forecast forward. The forecast for week 6 was 1663, but the actual was 1850, so the model moves up for week 7 by 0.3 × (1850 − 1663.43) = 56.

worked.answer: (a) F6 ≈ 1663.43, about 1663 visitors. (b) F7 ≈ 1719.40, about 1719 visitors.

worked.title: SES · 2023 makeup Q3b: is SES possible? Compare with a moving average (10 marks)

problem.text: Consider the following time series data. [10 marks]
(i) Fit an exponential smoothing model, if possible. If not, state the reasons. (ii) Fit a suitable moving average of your choice. (iii) Compare the above models and conclude.

steps.label: Keywords
steps.text: 'If possible. If not, state the reasons' is a test of whether you check the conditions first. 'Moving average of your choice': you pick k. 'Compare and conclude': error measure on the same years.

steps.label: (i) Is SES possible?
steps.text: Page 22: exponential smoothing is suitable with constant variance and no seasonality, for short-term forecasts. Page 23: with a strong trend it lags. This data is yearly (no seasonal pattern) and wanders around 15 to 21 with only a slow rise, so **yes, SES is possible.** Say these reasons in a line. If the data had climbed steadily (like the 50, 52, 54, 55, 57 sales) you would say SES lags and Holt is better.

steps.label: (i) Choose α: the question gives none
steps.text: No α is given, so you choose it, and you say how. The slides try three values and keep the smallest MSE (pages 11-15: α = 0.2, 0.4, 0.7). Same here, over 2017 to 2022: α = 0.2 gives MSE 8.43, **α = 0.4 gives 4.31**, α = 0.7 gives 5.74. So fit with α = 0.4.

steps.label: (iii) Compare on the same years (2017 to 2022)
steps.text: SES (α = 0.4) errors, actual − forecast: −1.16, 0.30, 1.18, 4.71, −0.17, 0.90; squares sum to 25.85, so **MSE = 4.31.** 3-year MA errors: −1, −1, 0, 5, 0, 0.33; squares sum to 27.11, so **MSE = 4.52.**

steps.label: Conclude
steps.text: The two models are almost equal. SES with α = 0.4 has the slightly lower MSE (4.31 < 4.52), so it is marginally better on 2017 to 2022. Forecasts for 2023: SES 18.46 and MA 19.33 crores. What earns the marks is the method: check the conditions, choose α by trying values and keeping the smallest MSE, compare both models over the same years, and conclude from the numbers. If you compare over all nine years instead, the best α changes (about 0.6), so state your basis.

steps.label: Convention
steps.text: There is no answer key, so the numbers are my calculations, checked by recomputing. The MA is covered fully in the moving-average topic (pages 16-21).

worked.answer: SES is possible (no seasonality, no strong trend). No α is given, so try several and keep the best: α = 0.4 (MSE 4.31 over 2017-2022). It forecasts 18.46 for 2023; the 3-year MA (MSE 4.52) forecasts 19.33. The two are nearly equal; SES is marginally better.

flashcards.back: F(t+1) = α·Yt + (1 − α)·Ft, starting with F2 = Y1.

flashcards.front: What does α = 1 give? And α = 0? (page 3)
flashcards.back: α = 1: the forecast is just the last actual value (a naive forecast). α = 0: the forecast is just the previous forecast.

flashcards.front: Small α or large α for a series with sudden spikes? (page 10)
flashcards.back: Large α. It gives more weight to the current value, so the forecast reacts faster. Small α gives a smoother series.

flashcards.front: 'Initial forecast for the first period equals the first actual': what is the second forecast?
flashcards.back: The same number. F2 = α·Y1 + (1 − α)·F1 = Y1 when F1 = Y1.
error = actual − forecast. MSE = (sum of squared errors) / number of periods.

flashcards.front: Name the four error measures on page 9
flashcards.back: MSE, MAD (mean absolute deviation), MAPE (mean absolute percent error), LAD (largest absolute deviation).

flashcards.front: How do you choose between two α values?
flashcards.back: Compute the MSE for each and pick the smaller one.

flashcards.front: The question says 'forecast for July' and the data ends in June. How many rows is that?
flashcards.back: One more row than the data: July's forecast uses June's actual and June's forecast.

quiz.q: Which α makes the simple exponential smoothing forecast react fastest to the latest value?
quiz.explain: α = 1 puts all the weight on the latest actual, a naive forecast (page 3).

quiz.q: In F(t+1) = α·Yt + (1 − α)·Ft, what does Ft stand for?
quiz.explain: Ft is the forecast made for period t; Yt is the actual.

quiz.q: To compare two smoothing constants you would use…
options: The one with the smaller MSE
The one with the larger MSE
quiz.explain: A smaller error means a better fit; the question asks you to justify with the MSE.

quiz.q: Demand 100, 110; F1 = 100; α = 0.5. What is F3, the forecast for the third period?
Initial forecast F(Jan) = 82, actuals Jan = 82 and Feb = 88, α = 0.4. What is F(Mar)?
Feb 2026 SES question, α = 0.7: what is the July forecast?
Sept 2025 SES question, α = 0.6: what is the 2022 forecast?
Sept 2025 SES question: what is the MSE for α = 0.3, dividing by all 7 years?
quiz.explain: Sum of squared errors 1472.29, divided by 7.

formulas.name: Forecast error and MSE
formulas.formula:
error = Yt − Ft
MSE = {{ Σ (Yt − Ft)² // number of periods }}

formulas.name: Other error measures
formulas.formula:
MAD = average of |error|
MAPE = average of |error| / Yt
LAD = largest |error|

families.label: SES
families.title: Simple exponential smoothing: forecast and compare α
families.lead: Asked in 2023, Sept 2025 and Feb 2026. Plug-and-play: build a table down the data.

items: 'Simple exponential smoothing', 'smoothing constant α', 'initial forecast equals …'.
A short table of actuals and a request to forecast the next period, often for two α values.

blocks.text: F(t+1) = α·Yt + (1 − α)·Ft          error = Yt − Ft          MSE = Σ error² / n

items: Note the start rule (initial forecast = first actual).
Write α and 1 − α.
Fill in the forecasts down the table, one row per period.
Add one row for the period to be forecast.
If asked to compare, compute the squared errors, add them, divide by n and pick the smaller MSE.
Write the justification line.

blocks.label: Remember
blocks.text: A larger α reacts faster (good for sudden spikes); a smaller α gives a smoother series.
